title: Generational slab reclamation with prefix fencing for GPU KV cache
creator: Marisol Chen
body:
Summary:
We need a new eviction/reclamation mechanism for the GPU-side KV cache that reduces fragmentation and uncontrolled OOMs while preserving prefix-scoped correctness guarantees used by continuous batching. The proposal is a generational slab allocator + checkpointed reclamation with a lightweight prefix fencing protocol so that in-flight batches referencing prefixes cannot observe partially reclaimed state.

Background and motivation:
- Current LRU/TTL and hybrid approaches work well for capacity trimming but create two problems on GPU: per-slab fragmentation (wasted GPU memory) and races between reclamation and concurrent batch KV lookups that can result in stale or missing prefix entries when cache metadata is compacted.
- Continuous batching increases concurrency: many requests share KV prefixes and KV cache reads happen from multiple worker threads/processors. We need atomicity at prefix granularity so a batch that begins with a prefix sees a coherent snapshot until it completes.
- Existing solutions (global eviction pause, coarse locks) hurt latency and throughput. We want a low-latency protocol that provides correctness guarantees with minimal blocking.

Goals and acceptance criteria:
1) Implement a generational slab allocator on the GPU that groups KV entries into short-lived generations. Slabs can be compacted/merged when all entries in a generation are safe to reclaim.
2) Provide a prefix-fence protocol: callers can acquire a cheap read-fence for a prefix (or prefix set) which ensures the underlying slab generation(s) referenced will not be reclaimed until the fence is released. Fences must be wait-free for the common path (no global stop-the-world).
3) Maintain existing external invariants: no request should observe a partially-evicted prefix (either full prefix present or logically absent), and KV lookup latency impact should be <5% p99 compared to baseline without fences.
4) Improve effective usable GPU memory by >=10% for production workloads with moderate churn (measured in internal perf harness).

Design overview:
- Generational slabs: allocate entries into current generation slab per shard. When a slab reaches a configured fullness or time window, new allocations move to a next generation. Each generation has a small header with an epoch id and a live-reference counter kept in host-managed pinned memory (fast atomic updates).
- Prefix metadata maps prefix -> list of (shard, generation id, offset, length, checksum). Lookups consult the map and then read from the slab.
- Prefix fence: a thread acquiring a prefix fence atomically increments the live-reference counter(s) for the generation(s) that the prefix maps to. This is a per-generation atomic counter update in CPU-visible pinned memory; no GPU kernel needed on the hot path. When a batch is done, it decrements the counters.
- Reclamation: background compactor scans generations with zero references and performs GPU-side compaction into new slabs or frees slabs. Compaction creates new slab placements and then atomically updates prefix metadata to point to the new locations; the switch is single atomic metadata update per prefix (using compare-and-swap on metadata version).
- Safety: the fence + compaction ordering ensures a reader either sees the pre-compaction data or the post-compaction data, not a mixture. The atomic CAS on metadata provides the commit point. Generations with non-zero counters will not be reclaimed.

Implementation plan (high level):
1) Prototype generation headers and per-generation counters in host pinned memory (week 1).
2) Extend prefix metadata to include generation ids and a small version integer (week 2).
3) Implement cheap fence acquire/release APIs used by continuous-batching read path; add microbench for read latency (week 2).
4) Implement background compactor that only touches zero-referenced generations (week 3).
5) Integrate atomic prefix metadata swap (CAS) and validate invariants with model checker + unit tests (week 4).
6) Run canary in a dedicated cluster with synthetic churn + production trace replay, gather telemetry and OOM/fragmentation metrics (week 5).

Performance and microbench expectations:
- Fence acquire/release should be 50-200ns on host (atomic inc/dec on pinned memory).
- Lookup fast path should avoid touching fences unless a caller explicitly requests prefix-fenced semantics. Default behavior remains best-effort LRU/TTL unless caller opts in.
- Background compaction bandwidth should be tunable; default rate = 1GB/s per compactor thread to avoid saturating PCIe.

Testing and correctness validation:
- Unit tests for fence semantics (acquire-count prevents reclamation).
- Fuzz tests: concurrent threads performing lookups, inserts, fence acquire/release, and compaction; assert no prefix returns partially-updated payloads and checksums validate.
- Model-checker run that verifies linearizability of prefix metadata CAS under concurrent fence operations.
- Integration test using continuous-batching harness with production traffic replay: verify <5% p99 latency regressions and improved usable memory.

Migration and rollout:
- Feature flag at shard-level to enable generational reclamation. Start in internal dedicated clusters (non-customer) then limited customer canaries (Dedicated tenants) for 2 weeks.
- Telemetry: track per-shard generation counts, average fence hold time, compaction throughput, p99 lookup latency, and fragmentation percent.
- Rollback plan: revert flag and drain compaction queue; compactor must be idempotent.

Risks and open questions:
- Atomicity guarantees depend on reliable CAS on metadata. We need to ensure metadata writes are durable and visible across processes in private deployments.
- Fences introduce additional host CPU memory traffic under extremely high concurrency; need to validate CPU overhead and potential contention hotspots. Potential mitigation: sharded counters per CPU core and periodic aggregation.
- Interop with existing TTL eviction and LRU fast-paths needs careful ordering: we must ensure that TTL expiry marks entries as "candidate" but does not free the generation until counters are zero.

Acceptance checklist:
- [ ] Prototype counters and fence API merged behind feature flag.
- [ ] Compactor implementation with generation scan and safe free.
- [ ] Comprehensive unit + fuzz + model-check tests passing.
- [ ] Canary run shows memory improvement >=10% and p99 lookup regression <5%.
- [ ] Design doc and runbook published.

Runbook snippets (for incidents):
- If compactor accidentally frees active generation (should not happen): immediately toggle feature flag off, restart compactor, run a consistency rescan to reconcile prefix metadata against slab manifest. Notify infra oncall.
- If fence counters show abnormal growth: inspect actor hold traces, collect stack samples from holding threads, and consider lowering default fence TTL for long-lived batches.

References and related work:
- Prior eviction designs: ENG-33421 (formalize-eviction-invariants-prefix-aware-hybrid)
- Compaction/shard reclamation: ENG-30642 (epoch-hybrid-kv-eviction)

Notes: This ticket focuses on correctness-first implementation; later optimizations (per-core counters, aggregated fencing, GPU-accelerated compaction kernels) will be separate follow-ups.

2026-03-09 - SRE, Tomasz Nowak: Raised concern about compactor IO on PCIe during peak. Suggested limiting compaction to off-peak or use rate-limiter token bucket. Added to implementation plan.
